voice.reference_text: 大家好，欢迎来到 AI 高频词。每一期，我们只讲清楚一个词：它解决什么问题，怎么理解它，以及它在现实里意味着什么。

items.text: A model's near-perfect on the data it learned from, then fails on new data.
Usually that's not a bug in the code. It's a problem called overfitting.
Overfitting is when a model learns its practice data too literally, flukes and all, so it does worse on new data.
Picture a student who memorizes every answer in the workbook, misprints included, and scores a hundred every time.
But on the exam, the questions change just a little, and he's lost.
The workbook is the model's data, and the misprints are what we call noise.
When a model memorizes the noise as if it were a real pattern, that's overfitting.
Let's see it happen. These ten points are our training data, our practice questions.
They roughly follow a pattern, but each one is nudged off by a bit of random wobble. That wobble is the noise.
The model's job is to find that pattern and predict new points.
The first model is too simple. It can only draw a straight line.
The farther a point is from the line, the bigger the mistake. The average mistake is the error.
The line can't even get the practice questions right. That's called underfitting.
The second model is a gentle curve. It misses some points, but it catches the overall trend.
The third is really complicated, twisting and turning through every single point, so its practice error is zero.
So which one do you think will do best on new questions?
Now we test them on six points they've never seen. That's the test data, our exam.
The second model stays close to all of them, so it does best.
The third zigzags between the practice points and misses some new points by a lot.
Its exam error is more than twenty times the second model's.
That's because it memorized the noise, and noise is random, so it doesn't repeat on new questions. That's overfitting.
Underfitting is easy to spot: it does badly on practice and exam questions.
Overfitting is sneakier, because its practice score can look amazing. Here, its practice error was zero.
Here's another way to see it: think of learning as compression.
To remember these ten points exactly, you'd need to store ten numbers, one height per point.
The second curve takes just four numbers, yet stays close to the points and predicts new ones well. That's compression.
The third curve needs ten numbers to go through ten points.
Ten numbers for ten points is no compression at all, so the noise got saved too.
Good compression keeps the pattern and throws out the noise. Squeeze too hard, like that straight line, and you lose the pattern too.
Take Google Flu Trends. Google once used people's searches to estimate what share of doctor visits involved flu-like symptoms.
At first, it sifted fifty million search terms to match about eleven hundred flu data points.
With far more terms than data points, it was bound to pick up some that just happened to spike in winter.
Researchers said this was overfitting. It was part flu detector, part winter detector.
Later versions missed too. In a hundred out of a hundred and eight weeks, they guessed too high.
How do you spot overfitting and stop it? Here are three common ways.
First, set aside some data as a mock exam, called a validation set.
Use it to pick your model and catch overfitting early. Save the real exam for the very end.
To be honest, in our experiment we picked the model by its exam score. On a real project, you shouldn't.
Second, collect more data, and more varied data, so noise and coincidences are less likely to pass for patterns.
Third, give the model a rule: overly complicated curves get penalized, so it won't chase the noise. That's called regularization.
Overfitting is memorizing the misprints and mistaking them for real patterns.
So whenever you feel like you totally get something, try a question you've never seen.
And in the next episode, we'll get into reinforcement learning.
